title: Στεινωπός
titleEn: Antilochus in the Narrow Road — Iliad 23.373–481
about: The teams come round the post and turn for home, and the mares of Eumelus lead until Apollo, angry at Diomedes, knocks the whip from his hand. Diomedes weeps with rage, but Athena gives the whip back, breaks Eumelus’ yoke, and sends him sprawling in the dust, scraped and speechless. Diomedes sweeps into the lead with Menelaus behind him. Antilochus urges Nestor’s old horses on with a threat of what his father will do, then sees his chance where a gully has cut the road down to a single chariot’s width, and drives on past Menelaus’ warning. Menelaus lets him go rather than risk a crash, and curses him with a hint that he will demand an oath. On the stand Idomeneus is the first to make out the leaders, guesses at the wrong driver, and is shouted down by Ajax son of Oileus, who insists that Eumelus’ mares are still in front.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ πύματον τέλεον δρόμον ὠκέες ἵπποι
ἂψ ἐφ’ ἁλὸς πολιῆς,
sentences.l:
But when indeed the last, the finishing run the swift horses
back to the grey sea,
sentences.i: But when the swift horses were on the last stretch of the course, the run back to the grey sea,
sentences.n: The race has turned at the post and is now on the home stretch, the run back toward the sea and the ships. The sentence has no verb of its own: ‘were running’ is understood, and the main clause comes in the next unit. τέλεον (‘final, finishing’) and πύματον (‘last’) are two words for the one stretch; τέλεον is the epic form of Attic τέλειος. ἁλὸς πολιῆς ‘the grey sea’ is the stock phrase, and ἐπί with the genitive here means ‘toward’. The part opens at the start of a printed paragraph.

sentences.t:
τότε δὴ ἀρετή γε ἑκάστου
φαίνετ’, ἄφαρ δ’ ἵπποισι τάθη δρόμος·
sentences.l:
then indeed the excellence of each
showed itself, and at once the run was stretched out for the horses;
sentences.i: then each horse’s excellence showed itself, and at once the run was stretched out for them;
sentences.n: τότε δή ‘then indeed’ answers the ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή of the last unit. ἀρετή is ‘excellence’, what a horse or man can do at its best, and ἑκάστου ‘of each’ leaves open whether it is horse or driver. φαίνετ’ is the unaugmented imperfect of φαίνομαι ‘show itself’, and τάθη, the aorist passive of τείνω ‘stretch’, is used of the race itself drawn out to full length, δρόμος ‘run’ being its subject. ἄφαρ ‘at once’ is an epic adverb.

sentences.t:
ὦκα δ’ ἔπειτα
αἳ Φηρητιάδαο ποδώκεες ἔκφερον ἵπποι.
sentences.l:
and quickly then
the mares of Pheres’-son, swift-footed, bore out ahead.
sentences.i: and then, quickly, the swift-footed mares of Pheres’ son drew out in front.
sentences.n: Φηρητιάδαο is a patronymic, ‘of the son of Pheres’, with the epic genitive ending -αο. Pheres’ son is Admetus, and the mares, as the next lines show, are driven by his son Eumelus. ποδώκεες ‘swift-footed’ is the stock epithet for horses, and ἔκφερον is the imperfect of ἐκφέρω ‘bear out’, used of a team that carries its driver out in front. αἳ is feminine, which tells us that the team is of mares.

sentences.t:
τὰς δὲ μετ’ ἐξέφερον Διομήδεος ἄρσενες ἵπποι
Τρώϊοι, οὐδέ τι πολλὸν ἄνευθ’ ἔσαν, ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ἐγγύς·
sentences.l:
and after them bore out Diomedes’ male horses,
the Trojan ones, and not at all far apart were they, but very near;
sentences.i: and after them came Diomedes’ stallions, the Trojan horses, and they were not far off at all, but very close;
sentences.n: τὰς δὲ μετ’ ‘and after them’ refers to the mares. The ἄρσενες ἵπποι ‘male horses’ are the two Diomedes won from Aeneas, and they are Τρώϊοι ‘Trojan’ (the diaeresis is as the edition prints it). ἐξέφερον is the same verb as in the line before. ἄνευθ’ ἔσαν ‘were apart’ has the old plural ἔσαν (= ἦσαν), and ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ἐγγύς ‘but very near’ closes the thought at the colon.

sentences.t:
αἰεὶ γὰρ δίφρου ἐπιβησομένοισιν ἐΐκτην,
πνοιῇ δ’ Εὐμήλοιο μετάφρενον εὐρέε τ’ ὤμω
θέρμετ’· ἐπ’ αὐτῷ γὰρ κεφαλὰς καταθέντε πετέσθην.
sentences.i: for all the time they looked as if about to climb into the chariot, and Eumelus’ back and his two broad shoulders were warmed by their breath, since they flew with their heads laid right over him.
sentences.n: Diomedes’ two horses are so close behind Eumelus’ chariot that they seem about to climb into it. ἐΐκτην is the dual of the perfect of ἔοικα ‘be like, seem’, and the dative plural ἐπιβησομένοισιν ‘to ones about to mount’ is what they are like, so the sense is ‘they seemed as men about to step up into the chariot’. θέρμετ’ is the passive of θέρμω ‘warm’, with the two subjects μετάφρενον ‘back’ and the dual εὐρέε … ὤμω ‘two broad shoulders’, and πνοιῇ is ‘by the breath’. καταθέντε is the dual aorist participle ‘having laid down’, and πετέσθην is the dual of ‘they flew’, unaugmented.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κεν ἢ παρέλασσ’ ἢ ἀμφήριστον ἔθηκεν,
εἰ μὴ Τυδέος υἷϊ κοτέσσατο Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων,
ὅς ῥά οἱ ἐκ χειρῶν ἔβαλεν μάστιγα φαεινήν.
sentences.i: And now he would either have driven past or left the race in dispute, had Phoebus Apollo not borne a grudge against the son of Tydeus and knocked the shining whip out of his hands.
sentences.n: καί νύ κεν … is a contrary-to-fact sentence in the epic manner: κεν with the aorist ἔθηκεν, ‘would have made’, and εἰ μή ‘if not’ giving the reason it did not happen. παρέλασσ’ is the aorist of παρελαύνω ‘drive past’, and ἀμφήριστον is ‘disputed on both sides’, a dead heat. The subject, never named, is Diomedes. Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων is the stock pair, and κοτέσσατο is the aorist middle of κοτέω ‘bear a grudge’, with the dative Τυδέος υἷϊ. ὅς ῥά οἱ ‘who … to him’ goes on in the relative: Apollo knocked the whip out of Diomedes’ hands.

sentences.t:
τοῖο δ’ ἀπ’ ὀφθαλμῶν χύτο δάκρυα χωομένοιο,
οὕνεκα τὰς μὲν ὅρα ἔτι καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον ἰούσας,
οἳ δέ οἱ ἐβλάφθησαν ἄνευ κέντροιο θέοντες.
sentences.l:
and from his eyes poured tears, of him enraged,
because he saw those mares still going and much faster,
but his own were hindered, running without a goad.
sentences.i: Tears of rage poured from his eyes, because he saw the others still going, and much faster, while his own horses were hampered, running without the goad.
sentences.n: τοῖο … χωομένοιο is a genitive absolute-like phrase, ‘of him incensed’, set after the tears. χύτο is the unaugmented aorist middle of χέω ‘pour’. ὅρα is the unaugmented imperfect of ὁράω ‘see’, and τὰς are the mares and the other team, which he still sees going and ἰούσας ‘going’ faster. ἐβλάφθησαν is the aorist passive of βλάπτω, ‘were hindered, put out of their stride’; οἳ, a masculine relative-looking pronoun, stands for Diomedes’ own horses. κέντρον is the goad, which the whip had replaced in his hand.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ Ἀθηναίην ἐλεφηράμενος λάθ’ Ἀπόλλων
Τυδεΐδην, μάλα δ’ ὦκα μετέσσυτο ποιμένα λαῶν,
δῶκε δέ οἱ μάστιγα, μένος δ’ ἵπποισιν ἐνῆκεν·
sentences.i: But Apollo, cheating the son of Tydeus, did not escape Athena’s notice; she darted swiftly after the shepherd of the people, gave him back his whip, and put might into his horses;
sentences.n: Athena has been watching, and answers the god’s trick. οὐδ’ ἄρ’ … λάθ’ ‘nor did he escape her notice’ takes the accusative Ἀθηναίην, and ἐλεφηράμενος is a rare participle meaning ‘cheating, tricking’, here of what Apollo did to Diomedes. μετέσσυτο is the aorist middle of μετασεύομαι ‘rush after’. ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is the stock phrase, here for Diomedes, and the subject of ‘gave’ and ‘put’ is Athena, whom the Greek does not name until the next unit. ἐνῆκεν is the aorist of ἐνίημι ‘put into’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ μετ’ Ἀδμήτου υἱὸν κοτέουσ’ ἐβεβήκει,
ἵππειον δέ οἱ ἦξε θεὰ ζυγόν· αἳ δέ οἱ ἵπποι
ἀμφὶς ὁδοῦ δραμέτην, ῥυμὸς δ’ ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἐλύσθη.
sentences.l:
and she went after Admetus’ son, bearing a grudge,
and she broke the horses’ yoke for him, the goddess; and his mares
ran off to the side of the road, and the pole was rolled to the ground.
sentences.i: and she, bearing a grudge, went after the son of Admetus, and the goddess broke his yoke; his mares ran off to the side of the road, and the pole was dragged down to the ground.
sentences.n: ἣ δέ is Athena, κοτέουσ’ ‘bearing a grudge’ is the participle of κοτέω, and Ἀδμήτου υἱόν is Eumelus (see 376). ἵππειον … ζυγόν is ‘the horses’ yoke’, and ἦξε is the aorist of ἄγνυμι ‘break’; the Greek calls her θεά after the verb. ἀμφὶς ὁδοῦ ‘to either side of the road’ is a loose phrase, and δραμέτην is the dual aorist of τρέχω. ῥυμός is the pole of the chariot, which falls to the ground, and ἐλύσθη is the aorist passive of εἰλύω ‘roll, wrap’, so the pole is rolled or dragged along the earth.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἐκ δίφροιο παρὰ τροχὸν ἐξεκυλίσθη,
ἀγκῶνάς τε περιδρύφθη στόμα τε ῥῖνάς τε,
θρυλίχθη δὲ μέτωπον ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι·
sentences.i: and he himself was rolled out of the chariot beside the wheel, scraped raw at the elbows, mouth and nostrils, and battered in the forehead above the brows;
sentences.n: Line 394 is word for word a line of Book 6 that also describes a driver thrown from his chariot; the first line takes that unit’s English, though the sentence goes on differently here. αὐτός ‘he himself’ is Eumelus, and ἐξεκυλίσθη is the aorist passive of ἐκκυλίω ‘roll out’. περιδρύφθη (‘was scraped all over’) takes the accusatives ἀγκῶνας, στόμα and ῥῖνας as parts affected, and θρυλίχθη (‘was battered’) is a rare verb. ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι ‘at the brows’ says where on the forehead.

sentences.t:
τὼ δέ οἱ ὄσσε
δακρυόφι πλῆσθεν, θαλερὴ δέ οἱ ἔσχετο φωνή.
sentences.l:
and his two eyes
were filled with tears, and his full voice was checked.
sentences.i: and his eyes filled with tears, and his strong voice was choked.
sentences.n: This line, with its first half, is word for word in the Odyssey, where the one weeping is a woman; here the grieving, bruised man is Eumelus, so οἱ is ‘his’. ὄσσε is the dual of ‘eyes’, and δακρυόφι is the epic dative-ending -φι (= δάκρυσι), ‘with tears’. πλῆσθεν is the unaugmented aorist passive of πίμπλημι ‘fill’, with the ending -εν for -ησαν. θαλερή ‘full’ describes the voice, and ἔσχετο is the aorist middle of ἔχω, ‘was checked’.

sentences.t:
Τυδεΐδης δὲ παρατρέψας ἔχε μώνυχας ἵππους,
πολλὸν τῶν ἄλλων ἐξάλμενος· ἐν γὰρ Ἀθήνη
ἵπποις ἧκε μένος καὶ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ κῦδος ἔθηκε.
sentences.l:
And the Tydeus’-son, turning aside, held the solid-hoofed horses,
far leaping out ahead of the others; for into them Athena
sent might, and upon him set glory.
sentences.i: And the son of Tydeus swerved aside and drove the solid-hoofed horses on, leaping far out ahead of the rest; for Athena had put might into his horses and set glory on the driver himself.
sentences.n: Diomedes now has his whip back and Athena has put new strength into his team. παρατρέψας ‘turning aside’ is the aorist participle of παρατρέπω, and ἔχε is the imperfect of ἔχω used for ‘kept on, drove’; μώνυχας ἵππους ‘solid-hoofed horses’ is the stock phrase. ἐξάλμενος ‘leaping out’ is an aorist middle participle of ἐξάλλομαι, said of the horses’ springing stride. ἐν … ἧκε is ‘put into’ with the preverb apart (tmesis), μένος ‘might’ going into the horses, and ἐπ’ αὐτῷ κῦδος ἔθηκε ‘set glory upon him’ is the same phrase Antilochus will use in 406.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ Ἀτρεΐδης εἶχε ξανθὸς Μενέλαος.
sentences.l: and after him held on Atreus’-son, fair-haired Menelaus.
sentences.i: and after him came the son of Atreus, fair-haired Menelaus.
sentences.n: τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ ‘and after him’ is the phrase of the start of the race, now said of the order of the teams. Ἀτρεΐδης is the patronymic for Menelaus, and ξανθὸς Μενέλαος ‘fair-haired Menelaus’ is the stock pair, translated every time. εἶχε is ‘held on his way’, as ἔχε in 398.

sentences.t: Ἀντίλοχος δ’ ἵπποισιν ἐκέκλετο πατρὸς ἑοῖο·
sentences.l: And Antilochus called out to the horses of his own father:
sentences.i: Antilochus called out to his father’s horses:
sentences.n: Antilochus is Nestor’s son, driving the old Pylos team of 23.303. ἐκέκλετο is the reduplicated aorist middle of κέλομαι ‘call on, urge’, as in Antilochus’ own chariot-calling at 23.371, and the dative ἵπποισιν ‘to the horses’ is what he calls to. πατρὸς ἑοῖο ‘of his own father’ has the possessive ἑός in the epic genitive -οιο, not a relative. The colon introduces his speech.

sentences.t: ἔμβητον καὶ σφῶϊ· τιταίνετον ὅττι τάχιστα.
sentences.l: “Step in, you two also, and stretch out as fast as possible.
sentences.i: “Get into it, you two as well, and stretch out as fast as you can.
sentences.n: The horses are addressed in the dual, as ‘you two’, all the way through the speech: ἔμβητον and τιταίνετον are dual imperatives. ἔμβητον is the aorist imperative of ἐμβαίνω ‘step in’, here ‘get into the race, join in’, and its sense is a little loose; σφῶϊ is the dual ‘you two’, and καί says ‘you too’, not only the others. τιταίνετον ‘stretch (yourselves out)’ takes up the stretching of the run in 375. ὅττι τάχιστα is the stock phrase ‘as quickly as possible’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι μὲν κείνοισιν ἐριζέμεν οὔ τι κελεύω
Τυδεΐδεω ἵπποισι δαΐφρονος, οἷσιν Ἀθήνη
νῦν ὤρεξε τάχος καὶ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ κῦδος ἔθηκεν·
sentences.i: To be sure, I do not tell you to compete with those horses of the son of Tydeus, the wise-hearted man, to whom Athena has now given speed and set glory on the driver himself;
sentences.n: ἤτοι μὲν … οὔ τι κελεύω ‘indeed I do not at all bid’ concedes that Diomedes’ team cannot be beaten head-on, and ἐριζέμεν (‘to quarrel, vie’) is the infinitive of ἐρίζω. κείνοισιν … ἵπποισι is ‘with those horses’, ἵπποισι being the epic dative plural, and Τυδεΐδεω is the epic genitive of the patronymic Τυδεΐδης, ‘of the son of Tydeus’. δαΐφρονος is the stock epithet, ‘wise-minded’ in l and ‘wise-hearted’ in i, some say ‘fierce’ instead. ὤρεξε is the aorist of ὀρέγω ‘hold out, offer’, and ἐπ’ αὐτῷ κῦδος ἔθηκεν repeats the phrase of 400.

sentences.t:
ἵππους δ’ Ἀτρεΐδαο κιχάνετε, μὴ δὲ λίπησθον,
καρπαλίμως, μὴ σφῶϊν ἐλεγχείην καταχεύῃ
Αἴθη θῆλυς ἐοῦσα·
sentences.i: But catch up with the horses of the son of Atreus and do not fall behind, quickly, or Aethe, a mere female, will heap disgrace on you;
sentences.n: ἵππους δ’ Ἀτρεΐδαο ‘but the horses of Atreus’ son’ sets the real target against the impossible one before it; Ἀτρεΐδαο is the epic genitive of the patronymic (Menelaus). κιχάνετε is the present imperative of κιχάνω ‘overtake’, plural in form though two horses are meant, while μὴ δὲ λίπησθον is dual: the aorist subjunctive middle of λείπω, ‘do not be left behind’. μὴ … καταχεύῃ is a ‘lest’ clause, ‘lest she pour down’, and ἐλεγχείην is ‘disgrace, reproach’. Αἴθη is Agamemnon’s mare, now in Menelaus’ team (23.295); θῆλυς ἐοῦσα ‘being female’ is the jibe, that mares will beat horses.

sentences.t: τί ἢ λείπεσθε φέριστοι;
sentences.l: why, then, are you left behind, best of horses?
sentences.i: Why, then, are you falling behind, you best of horses?
sentences.n: τί ἤ ‘why then?’ is a lively question, and λείπεσθε is the present middle (passive) of λείπω, ‘are left behind’. φέριστοι is the vocative plural of φέριστος ‘best’, the superlative of φέρτερος, here said to the horses by way of both reproach and praise; the Greek of the same word to men is ‘best of men’.

sentences.t: ὧδε γὰρ ἐξερέω, καὶ μὴν τετελεσμένον ἔσται·
sentences.l: for thus I will declare, and truly accomplished it will be;
sentences.i: For this I will declare, and it will surely be accomplished:
sentences.n: This line is word for word a line of the Odyssey, and takes its English. ἐξερέω is the future of ἐξερέω ‘declare’, with the epic ending, καὶ μὴν ‘and truly’ gives force, and τετελεσμένον ἔσται is a future perfect made of the perfect passive participle of τελέω ‘accomplish’ and the verb ‘to be’. The threat Antilochus now makes is a real one.

sentences.t:
οὐ σφῶϊν κομιδὴ παρὰ Νέστορι ποιμένι λαῶν
ἔσσεται, αὐτίκα δ’ ὔμμε κατακτενεῖ ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
αἴ κ’ ἀποκηδήσαντε φερώμεθα χεῖρον ἄεθλον.
sentences.l:
no care for you two will there be with Nestor, shepherd of the people,
but at once he will kill you two with the sharp bronze,
if through slackness we carry off a worse contest-prize.
sentences.i: You will get no tending from Nestor, shepherd of the people; he will kill you on the spot with the sharp bronze, if we grow slack and carry off a worse prize.
sentences.n: κομιδή is ‘care, tending’ and σφῶϊν is the dual ‘for you two’; ἔσσεται is the future of εἰμί with the doubled σ. Νέστορι ποιμένι λαῶν ‘Nestor, shepherd of the people’ is the stock phrase. The threat is that the horses would be put down at once, αὐτίκα ‘at once’ with κατακτενεῖ, the future of κατακτείνω ‘kill’, and ὔμμε is the Aeolic-looking accusative ‘you two’ (= ὑμέας). ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ ‘with the sharp bronze’ is the stock phrase. αἴ κ’ = εἰ κε ‘if’, and ἀποκηδήσαντε is the dual aorist participle of ἀποκηδέω, ‘grown careless, slackened’, in the plural-dual loose agreement with φερώμεθα ‘we carry off’, an aorist subjunctive. ἄεθλον is a contest-prize here, not the contest.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐφομαρτεῖτον καὶ σπεύδετον ὅττι τάχιστα·
sentences.l: But keep up with them and hurry as fast as possible;
sentences.i: But keep up with them and hurry as quickly as you can;
sentences.n: ἐφομαρτεῖτον is the dual imperative of ἐφομαρτέω ‘go along with, keep close behind’, and σπεύδετον is the dual imperative of σπεύδω ‘hurry’. ὅττι τάχιστα ‘as quickly as possible’ is used again, as in 403. The semicolon-like high stop after τάχιστα turns the order from the threat to the plan of the next two lines.

sentences.t:
ταῦτα δ’ ἐγὼν αὐτὸς τεχνήσομαι ἠδὲ νοήσω
στεινωπῷ ἐν ὁδῷ παραδύμεναι, οὐδέ με λήσει.
sentences.l:
and this I myself will contrive and devise
to slip past in a narrow road, and it will not escape me.”
sentences.i: I will see to that myself, and work out how to slip past in a narrow part of the road, and the chance will not escape me.”
sentences.n: ταῦτα ‘this’ is the plan, and the infinitive παραδύμεναι (the epic form, = παραδῦναι) tells what the plan is: ‘to slip past’. τεχνήσομαι ‘I will contrive’ (from τέχνη, art or craft) and νοήσω ‘I will think out’ fit what Nestor taught the boy at 23.306 ff: win by cunning, not strength. στεινωπῷ ἐν ὁδῷ is ‘in a narrow road’, a first look at the place of the next lines, and οὐδέ με λήσει ‘and it will not escape me’ (the opportunity) has the same shape as the Odyssey’s οὐδέ σε λήσει. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δὲ ἄνακτος ὑποδείσαντες ὁμοκλὴν
μᾶλλον ἐπιδραμέτην ὀλίγον χρόνον·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they, fearing the rebuke of the lord,
the harder ran on for a short time;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they, afraid of their lord’s shouted rebuke, ran on harder for a little while;
sentences.n: The first line is word for word a line of Book 12, where the sentence goes on differently, and takes that unit’s English for the line. ὣς ἔφαθ’ is the unaugmented aorist of φημί, ‘so he spoke’, and οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the horses. ἄνακτος is the epic genitive of ἄναξ, ‘lord’, here Antilochus as the horses’ master, and ὁμοκλήν is the ‘rebuke’ (a threatening shout, from ὁμοκλάω ‘shout at’). ἐπιδραμέτην is the dual aorist of ἐπιτρέχω ‘run on’, and ὀλίγον χρόνον is accusative of time, ‘for a little time’.

sentences.t:
αἶψα δ’ ἔπειτα
στεῖνος ὁδοῦ κοίλης ἴδεν Ἀντίλοχος μενεχάρμης.
sentences.l:
and soon then
a narrow place of the hollow road saw Antilochus, steadfast in the fray.
sentences.i: and soon Antilochus, steadfast in the fray, saw a narrow place in the sunken road.
sentences.n: αἶψα δ’ ἔπειτα ‘and soon then’ marks the moment the plan meets its chance. στεῖνος (‘narrow place’, neuter) has the genitive ὁδοῦ κοίλης, ‘of a hollow road’, a road sunk below the ground on either side. Ἀντίλοχος μενεχάρμης is the stock pair for Antilochus: μενεχάρμης is ‘steadfast in the fray’, from μένω ‘stand fast’ and χάρμη ‘fight’. The word order puts the subject after the verb, ἴδεν (unaugmented aorist of ὁράω).

sentences.t:
ῥωχμὸς ἔην γαίης, ᾗ χειμέριον ἀλὲν ὕδωρ
ἐξέρρηξεν ὁδοῖο, βάθυνε δὲ χῶρον ἅπαντα·
sentences.l:
There was a gully of the earth, where winter water, having gathered,
had burst out part of the road, and deepened the whole place;
sentences.i: There was a gully in the ground, where winter water, collecting there, had torn away part of the road and sunk the whole spot deeper;
sentences.n: ῥωχμός is a ‘cleft, gully’, and ἔην is the epic form of ‘there was’. χειμέριον … ὕδωρ is ‘winter water’, meaning water from the winter rains, and ἀλέν is the aorist passive participle of εἴλω (‘pressed together, gathered’) with the neuter ὕδωρ. ἐξέρρηξεν ὁδοῖο ‘burst out (part) of the road’ has a partitive genitive, with the epic ending -οιο, and βάθυνε is the unaugmented imperfect ‘deepened’ (χῶρον ἅπαντα ‘the whole spot’). The road is hollow because of this water.

sentences.t: τῇ ῥ’ εἶχεν Μενέλαος ἁματροχιὰς ἀλεείνων.
sentences.l: that way held Menelaus, avoiding wheel-clashes.
sentences.i: That was the way Menelaus held to, so as to avoid a clash of wheels.
sentences.n: τῇ ῥ’ is ‘there, by that way’, and εἶχεν is ‘held on’, as in 401. ἁματροχιάς is a rare word for the ‘running together of wheels’, that is, a clash or locking of chariot-wheels; ἀλεείνων is the present participle of ἀλεείνω ‘avoid’. Menelaus keeps to the line along the gully, where there is only room for one chariot, so that nobody can crowd him.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχος δὲ παρατρέψας ἔχε μώνυχας ἵππους
ἐκτὸς ὁδοῦ, ὀλίγον δὲ παρακλίνας ἐδίωκεν.
sentences.l:
But Antilochus, turning aside, held the solid-hoofed horses
out of the road, and, leaning a little aside, pursued.
sentences.i: But Antilochus swerved aside and drove the solid-hoofed horses on, off the road, and, bending a little out of his way, gave chase.
sentences.n: Line 423 is word for word line 398, with Antilochus for the son of Tydeus, and takes the same English. ἐκτὸς ὁδοῦ is ‘outside the road’, and παρακλίνας is the aorist participle of παρακλίνω ‘bend aside’; ἐδίωκεν is ‘pursued’. Antilochus leaves the track for the open ground beside the gully and takes the wider line.

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδης δ’ ἔδεισε καὶ Ἀντιλόχῳ ἐγεγώνει·
sentences.l: And Atreus’-son was afraid and called aloud to Antilochus:
sentences.i: The son of Atreus was afraid and called out to Antilochus:
sentences.n: ἔδεισε is the aorist of δείδω ‘be afraid’, and ἐγεγώνει (‘called aloud to’) is the pluperfect used as an imperfect of γέγωνα, with the dative Ἀντιλόχῳ. Ἀτρεΐδης is Menelaus, who sees the danger of a crash.

sentences.t: Ἀντίλοχ’ ἀφραδέως ἱππάζεαι, ἀλλ’ ἄνεχ’ ἵππους·
sentences.l: “Antilochus, senselessly you drive horses; but hold the horses up;
sentences.i: “Antilochus, you are driving without sense; rein in your horses!
sentences.n: Ἀντίλοχ’ is the vocative with the final vowel elided. ἀφραδέως is the adverb ‘senselessly, without thought’, and ἱππάζεαι (‘you drive horses’) is the second singular middle in the open epic form -εαι, with no contraction. ἄνεχ’ is the imperative of ἀνέχω, ‘hold up, rein in’, taking the accusative ἵππους.

sentences.t:
στεινωπὸς γὰρ ὁδός, τάχα δ’ εὐρυτέρη παρελάσσαι·
μή πως ἀμφοτέρους δηλήσεαι ἅρματι κύρσας.
sentences.l:
for the road is narrow, and soon it is wider to drive past;
lest somehow you harm us both, striking with a chariot.”
sentences.i: The road is narrow, and soon it will be wider for passing; do not run into me and wreck us both.”
sentences.n: στεινωπός is ‘narrow’ and εὐρυτέρη is the comparative ‘wider’, with the infinitive παρελάσσαι ‘to drive past’ (the epic -σσ-). μή πως … δηλήσεαι is a ‘lest’ clause with the future-looking subjunctive ‘lest somehow you harm’, and ἀμφοτέρους means both of them. ἅρματι κύρσας (‘having struck with or against a chariot’) does not say whose chariot; the context is a collision. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἀντίλοχος δ’ ἔτι καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον ἔλαυνε
κέντρῳ ἐπισπέρχων ὡς οὐκ ἀΐοντι ἐοικώς.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, but Antilochus still and much more drove
urging with the goad, like one not hearing.
sentences.i: So he spoke, but Antilochus drove on still harder, urging his team on with the goad, like a man who had not heard.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so he spoke’, and ἔτι καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον ‘still, and much more’ shows that Antilochus drives harder after the warning, not softer. ἐπισπέρχων is the present participle of ἐπισπέρχω ‘urge on, press’, and κέντρῳ is the dative ‘with the goad’. ὡς οὐκ ἀΐοντι ἐοικώς is ‘like one not hearing’: ἐοικώς is the perfect participle of ἔοικα, ‘resembling’, and ἀΐοντι is the dative of the present participle of ἀΐω ‘hear’, so he acts as if he had heard nothing.

sentences.t:
ὅσσα δὲ δίσκου οὖρα κατωμαδίοιο πέλονται,
ὅν τ’ αἰζηὸς ἀφῆκεν ἀνὴρ πειρώμενος ἥβης,
τόσσον ἐπιδραμέτην·
sentences.i: As far as a discus carries when a strong man, testing his youth, has thrown it from the shoulder, so far did the two run on ahead;
sentences.n: ὅσσα … τόσσον ‘as great as … so great’ is a comparison of distance. οὖρα is a measure of length, here the reach of one cast; δίσκου κατωμαδίοιο is ‘of a discus hurled from the shoulder’, an adjective of κατὰ ὦμον. αἰζηός is a ‘vigorous young man’, ἀφῆκεν is the aorist of ἀφίημι (the ‘gnomic’ aorist, of what happens every time), and πειρώμενος ἥβης is ‘testing his youthful strength’, with the genitive. τόσσον ἐπιδραμέτην is the dual aorist, ‘the two ran on’, said of Antilochus’ horses.

sentences.t:
αἳ δ’ ἠρώησαν ὀπίσσω
Ἀτρεΐδεω·
sentences.l:
while the horses drew back, behind,
those of Atreus’-son;
sentences.i: while the horses of the son of Atreus drew back behind;
sentences.n: αἳ δ’ are the mares and horses of Menelaus’ team, with the genitive Ἀτρεΐδεω (epic -εω) after it, ‘those of Atreus’ son’, moved to the next line. ἠρώησαν is the aorist of ἐρωέω ‘draw back, hang back’ and ὀπίσσω is ‘behind’. This unit ends in the middle of line 434, and the next gives the reason.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς γὰρ ἑκὼν μεθέηκεν ἐλαύνειν
μή πως συγκύρσειαν ὁδῷ ἔνι μώνυχες ἵπποι,
δίφρους τ’ ἀνστρέψειαν ἐϋπλεκέας, κατὰ δ’ αὐτοὶ
ἐν κονίῃσι πέσοιεν ἐπειγόμενοι περὶ νίκης.
sentences.l:
for he himself willingly had let go the driving,
lest somehow they run together in the road, the solid-hoofed horses,
and overturn the well-plaited chariots, and themselves
fall in the dust, hastening for victory.
sentences.i: for he himself had let up in his driving, of his own will, afraid that the solid-hoofed horses might somehow collide in the road, overturn the finely plaited chariots, and the men themselves fall in the dust in their eagerness for victory.
sentences.n: Menelaus has chosen to hold back. αὐτός ‘he himself’ is Menelaus, ἑκών ‘willingly’, and μεθέηκεν is the aorist of μεθίημι ‘let go, let up’ with the infinitive ἐλαύνειν ‘from driving’. The three optatives, συγκύρσειαν, ἀνστρέψειαν (‘overturn’) and πέσοιεν, all depend on μή πως ‘lest somehow’, which is a fear clause. μώνυχες ἵπποι ‘solid-hoofed horses’ is the stock phrase and ἐϋπλεκέας ‘well-plaited’ (the diaeresis is printed) describes the woven chariot-bodies. αὐτοί ‘themselves’ are the drivers, and ἐπειγόμενοι περὶ νίκης is ‘pressing hard for victory’.

sentences.t: τὸν καὶ νεικείων προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.l: Him, rebuking, addressed fair-haired Menelaus:
sentences.i: Fair-haired Menelaus said to him, rebuking him:
sentences.n: τὸν … προσέφη ‘addressed him’ is the usual speech introduction, and νεικείων (‘rebuking’) says the tone, the present participle of νεικείω; καί here only strengthens the participle and is not translated. ξανθὸς Μενέλαος ‘fair-haired Menelaus’ is the stock pair. The colon introduces Menelaus’ second speech, to Antilochus.

sentences.t: Ἀντίλοχ’ οὔ τις σεῖο βροτῶν ὀλοώτερος ἄλλος·
sentences.l: “Antilochus, no other of mortals is more baleful than you;
sentences.i: “Antilochus, no other mortal is more baleful than you;
sentences.n: Ἀντίλοχ’ is the vocative, and οὔ τις … ἄλλος is ‘no other’, with βροτῶν ‘of mortals’ as the partitive genitive. σεῖο is the epic genitive of σύ, ‘than you’, after the comparative ὀλοώτερος, ‘more baleful, more ruinous’. Menelaus, who just held back for safety, is angry with the one who ignored his warning.

sentences.t:
ἔρρ’, ἐπεὶ οὔ σ’ ἔτυμόν γε φάμεν πεπνῦσθαι Ἀχαιοί.
ἀλλ’ οὐ μὰν οὐδ’ ὧς ἄτερ ὅρκου οἴσῃ ἄεθλον.
sentences.l:
go to ruin, since not truly did we say, we Achaeans, that you had sense;
but surely not even so will you carry off the contest-prize without an oath.”
sentences.i: Be off with you! We Achaeans were wrong to say you had any sense; but even so you will not carry off the prize without an oath.”
sentences.n: ἔρρ’ (ἔρρε) is the imperative of ἔρρω, ‘be gone, go to ruin’. φάμεν is the first plural of φημί, unaugmented, ‘we said’, and Ἀχαιοί ‘we Achaeans’ is the apposition; Menelaus includes the whole army in the mistaken praise. οὔ σ’ ἔτυμόν γε … πεπνῦσθαι is ‘that you had sense’, the perfect infinitive of πνέω in the sense ‘be sensible’, with the adverb ἔτυμον ‘truly’. In 441 ἀλλ’ οὐ μὰν οὐδ’ ὧς is ‘but surely not even so’, and ἄτερ ὅρκου is ‘without an oath’: Menelaus will make Antilochus swear that he did not foul him. οἴσῃ is the second singular future middle of φέρω.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ἵπποισιν ἐκέκλετο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.l: So having spoken, to the horses he called out and lifted his voice:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and called out to his horses, raising his voice:
sentences.n: This line is a stock introduction, word for word as in Book 8, and takes that unit’s English. ὣς εἰπών is the aorist participle ‘so having spoken’, ἐκέκλετο is ‘called out’ with the dative ἵπποισιν, and φώνησέν τε (‘and lifted his voice’) is the aorist of φωνέω. The horses are Menelaus’ own, and the colon introduces his speech to them.

sentences.t: μή μοι ἐρύκεσθον μὴ δ’ ἕστατον ἀχνυμένω κῆρ.
sentences.l: “Do not hold yourselves back for me, nor stand, grieving in heart.
sentences.i: “Do not hold back on me, and do not stand there grieving at heart.
sentences.n: Menelaus speaks to his two horses, in the dual, just as Antilochus did. ἐρύκεσθον is the dual imperative middle of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’, with μοι ‘for me’, and ἕστατον is the dual imperative of ἵστημι ‘stand’ (the perfect-stem form). ἀχνυμένω κῆρ ‘grieving in heart’ is the accusative of respect, and ἀχνυμένω is the dual participle; it is the phrase used of Achilles’ horses mourning Patroclus.

sentences.t:
φθήσονται τούτοισι πόδες καὶ γοῦνα καμόντα
ἢ ὑμῖν· ἄμφω γὰρ ἀτέμβονται νεότητος.
sentences.l:
Sooner will the feet and the knees of these grow weary
than yours; for both are cheated of youth.”
sentences.i: The feet and knees of those two will tire before yours do, for they are both cheated of their youth.”
sentences.n: φθήσονται is the future middle of φθάνω ‘be first’, and τούτοισι ‘for these’ means Antilochus’ old Pylos team; ὑμῖν ‘yours’ is Menelaus’ horses, the comparison coming after ἤ ‘than’. πόδες καὶ γοῦνα καμόντα ‘feet and knees, wearied’ has the neuter participle of κάμνω. ἄμφω ‘both’ are Nestor’s two horses, and ἀτέμβονται is the present passive of ἀτέμβω, ‘are cheated of, lack’, taking the genitive νεότητος ‘youth’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δὲ ἄνακτος ὑποδείσαντες ὁμοκλὴν
μᾶλλον ἐπιδραμέτην, τάχα δέ σφισιν ἄγχι γένοντο.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they, fearing the rebuke of the lord,
ran on the harder, and soon near them they came.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they, afraid of their lord’s shouted rebuke, ran on harder, and soon were close behind the others.
sentences.n: The first line is the line of 417 again, and takes the English it has there. μᾶλλον ἐπιδραμέτην ‘ran on the harder’ is as at 418, and τάχα δέ ‘and soon’ continues. σφισιν ‘to them’ is the other team, Antilochus’, and ἄγχι γένοντο is ‘came near’, with the old plural γένοντο in a sentence whose subject has just been dual.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι δ’ ἐν ἀγῶνι καθήμενοι εἰσορόωντο
ἵππους· τοὶ δὲ πέτοντο κονίοντες πεδίοιο.
sentences.l:
And the Argives, sitting in the gathering, looked at
the horses; and they flew, raising dust over the plain.
sentences.i: The Argives, sitting in the gathering, were watching the horses as they flew along, raising dust over the plain.
sentences.n: The poet turns to the crowd, who sit in the ἀγών, the ‘gathering’ that the Greeks make a ring round the course. Ἀργεῖοι ‘Argives’ is one of the poem’s three names for the whole army. εἰσορόωντο is the imperfect of εἰσοράω ‘look at’, the open form with -όω-, and τοὶ δέ is ‘and they’, the horses. πέτοντο ‘flew’ is the imperfect of πέτομαι, κονίοντες πεδίοιο ‘raising dust over the plain’ is the same phrase as at 371, and πεδίοιο is the epic genitive of place.

sentences.t:
πρῶτος δ’ Ἰδομενεὺς Κρητῶν ἀγὸς ἐφράσαθ’ ἵππους·
ἧστο γὰρ ἐκτὸς ἀγῶνος ὑπέρτατος ἐν περιωπῇ·
sentences.l:
and first Idomeneus, leader of the Cretans, noticed the horses;
for he sat outside the gathering, highest, on a lookout;
sentences.i: Idomeneus, leader of the Cretans, was the first to make out the horses; he was sitting outside the gathering, at the very top, on a lookout;
sentences.n: πρῶτος ‘first’ with ἐφράσαθ’, the aorist middle of φράζομαι ‘notice’, and Κρητῶν ἀγός ‘leader of the Cretans’ is the stock phrase for Idomeneus. ἧστο is the pluperfect (as imperfect) of ἧμαι ‘sit’; ἐκτὸς ἀγῶνος is ‘outside the gathering’ and ὑπέρτατος ‘highest’, so he can see farther than the rest. περιωπῇ is a ‘lookout, a place from which one sees round about’, with ἐν.

sentences.t:
τοῖο δ’ ἄνευθεν ἐόντος ὁμοκλητῆρος ἀκούσας
ἔγνω,
sentences.l:
and when he heard, from far off, the man shouting
he knew him,
sentences.i: and, hearing the driver shouting though he was far away, he knew him,
sentences.n: τοῖο … ἐόντος ὁμοκλητῆρος is a genitive ‘of the shouter, who was far off’, depending on ἀκούσας ‘having heard’. ὁμοκλητήρ is the ‘one who shouts at’, from ὁμοκλάω; the context makes it the driver urging his horses, though the Greek does not say which driver. ἄνευθεν ἐόντος is ‘being apart, at a distance’, and ἔγνω is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘recognise’. The unit ends in the middle of line 453.

sentences.t:
φράσσατο δ’ ἵππον ἀριπρεπέα προὔχοντα,
ὃς τὸ μὲν ἄλλο τόσον φοῖνιξ ἦν, ἐν δὲ μετώπῳ
λευκὸν σῆμα τέτυκτο περίτροχον ἠΰτε μήνη.
sentences.l:
and he noticed a horse, outstanding, forging ahead,
which in all the rest was crimson, and on the forehead
a white mark had been made, round as the moon.
sentences.i: and he made out a horse that stood out as it forged ahead, crimson all over except for a white mark on its forehead, made round like the moon.
sentences.n: φράσσατο is the same aorist middle as ἐφράσαθ’, ‘noticed’. ἵππον ἀριπρεπέα προὔχοντα is ‘a horse, outstanding, forging ahead’; ἀριπρεπής ‘outstanding’ and προὔχοντα, for προέχοντα, ‘standing out in front’. φοῖνιξ is ‘crimson’ (a dark red), here of the horse’s coat, with the adverbs τὸ μὲν ἄλλο τόσον meaning ‘in all the rest’. σῆμα τέτυκτο (‘a mark had been made’) is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω, περίτροχον ‘round’, and ἠΰτε μήνη is ‘like the moon’. The horse is only a way of recognising the team, the trait which Idomeneus will mistakenly place with the wrong driver.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ὀρθὸς καὶ μῦθον ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.l: and he stood upright and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.i: He stood up straight and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.n: This line is word for word the line that introduces Achilles’ speech at 23.271, and takes its English. στῆ is the aorist of ἵστημι ‘stood’, ὀρθός ‘upright’ and μῦθον … ἔειπεν ‘spoke a word’ is a formula, and ἐν Ἀργείοισιν is ‘among the Argives’. The colon introduces Idomeneus’ speech.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι Ἀργείων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες
οἶος ἐγὼν ἵππους αὐγάζομαι ἦε καὶ ὑμεῖς;
sentences.l:
“O friends, leaders and lords of the Argives,
is it I alone who make out the horses, or you also?
sentences.i: “Friends, leaders and lords of the Argives, am I the only one who sees the horses, or do you too?
sentences.n: Line 457 is word for word a line of Book 2, where it opens Nestor’s answer on the dream, and takes that unit’s English for the line: φίλοι ‘friends’ and Ἀργείων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες ‘leaders and lords of the Argives’. In 458 οἶος ‘alone’ goes with ἐγών ‘I’, αὐγάζομαι is ‘catch sight of’, and ἦε is ‘or’ in a question, with καὶ ὑμεῖς ‘you also’. Idomeneus’ speech is a question put to the whole army.

sentences.t:
ἄλλοι μοι δοκέουσι παροίτεροι ἔμμεναι ἵπποι,
ἄλλος δ’ ἡνίοχος ἰνδάλλεται· αἳ δέ που αὐτοῦ
ἔβλαβεν ἐν πεδίῳ, αἳ κεῖσέ γε φέρτεραι ἦσαν·
sentences.i: Different horses seem to me to be in the lead, and a different driver shows himself; and the mares that were stronger out there have come to grief somewhere on the plain, I think;
sentences.n: ἄλλοι … ἵπποι ‘other horses’ and ἄλλος … ἡνίοχος ‘another charioteer’ both mean: not the ones I saw at the post. δοκέουσι is ‘seem’, with the open form, παροίτεροι ‘further forward’ (the comparative of πάρος-type adverb), and ἰνδάλλεται ‘appears, shows itself’. αἳ δέ are the mares he first saw ahead; αὐτοῦ ‘right there’ and που ‘somewhere, I suppose’ make the guess, and ἔβλαβεν is a short aorist passive of βλάπτω, ‘were hampered’, here with a plural subject. κεῖσέ γε ‘there, at least’, φέρτεραι ‘stronger’, ἦσαν ‘were’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι γὰρ τὰς πρῶτα ἴδον περὶ τέρμα βαλούσας,
νῦν δ’ οὔ πῃ δύναμαι ἰδέειν· πάντῃ δέ μοι ὄσσε
Τρωϊκὸν ἂμ πεδίον παπταίνετον εἰσορόωντι·
sentences.l:
For indeed those I saw first rounding the turning-post,
but now nowhere can I see them; and everywhere my two eyes
over the Trojan plain glance about, as I look.
sentences.i: I did see them first as they rounded the turning-post, but now I cannot see them anywhere; my eyes glance about everywhere over the Trojan plain as I look.
sentences.n: ἤτοι γάρ ‘for indeed’ gives the reason for the guess. τὰς are the mares, πρῶτα ἴδον ‘I saw first’ (unaugmented aorist of ὁράω), and περὶ τέρμα βαλούσας is ‘rounding the turning-post’, the participle of βάλλω with περί, said of horses that throw themselves round the mark. οὔ πῃ … ἰδέειν is ‘nowhere to see’, the epic infinitive. ὄσσε is the dual ‘two eyes’, with παπταίνετον the dual of παπταίνω ‘glance about’, and εἰσορόωντι is the dative ‘to me looking’. Τρωϊκὸν … πεδίον is the plain of Troy, as the Greeks’ games are held beside the ships.

sentences.t:
ἦε τὸν ἡνίοχον φύγον ἡνία, οὐδὲ δυνάσθη
εὖ σχεθέειν περὶ τέρμα καὶ οὐκ ἐτύχησεν ἑλίξας·
sentences.l:
Either the reins slipped away from the charioteer, and he was not able
to hold them well round the turning-post, and did not succeed in turning;
sentences.i: Either the reins slipped from the driver, and he could not hold them well at the turning-post, and failed to make the turn;
sentences.n: ἦε … is the first of Idomeneus’ two guesses for the missing horses. τὸν ἡνίοχον φύγον ἡνία is ‘the reins escaped the driver’, with φύγον the aorist of φεύγω and ἡνία the plural ‘reins’. δυνάσθη is the aorist passive of δύναμαι with the sense ‘was able’, σχεθέειν is the epic infinitive of ἔχω (‘hold’), and οὐκ ἐτύχησεν ἑλίξας is ‘did not succeed in turning’, with the aorist participle of ἑλίσσω ‘turn round’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά μιν ἐκπεσέειν ὀΐω σύν θ’ ἅρματα ἆξαι,
αἳ δ’ ἐξηρώησαν, ἐπεὶ μένος ἔλλαβε θυμόν.
sentences.l:
there, I think, he fell out and smashed the chariot,
and the mares drew back out, when might took hold of their spirit.
sentences.i: There, I think, he was thrown out and smashed the chariot, and the mares bolted off the course when their wild strength took hold of their spirit.
sentences.n: ἔνθα ‘there’ is at the turning-post, and μιν (‘him’) is the driver, the subject of ἐκπεσέειν ‘fell out’, the epic infinitive, after ὀΐω ‘I think’. σύν … ἆξαι is ‘smashed together’, the aorist of ἄγνυμι with the preverb apart (tmesis), and ἅρματα is plural for the one chariot. αἳ δ’ are the mares, ἐξηρώησαν the aorist of ἐρωέω with ἐκ-, ‘drew back out’, here ‘swerved out of the course’; μένος ‘might’ is their own wild strength, and ἔλλαβε is the epic aorist of λαμβάνω.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ ἴδεσθε καὶ ὔμμες ἀνασταδόν· οὐ γὰρ ἔγωγε
εὖ διαγιγνώσκω· δοκέει δέ μοι ἔμμεναι ἀνὴρ
Αἰτωλὸς γενεήν, μετὰ δ’ Ἀργείοισιν ἀνάσσει
Τυδέος ἱπποδάμου υἱὸς κρατερὸς Διομήδης.
sentences.l:
But look, you also, standing up; for I myself
do not know well; and it seems to me to be a man
an Aetolian by birth, and among the Argives he rules,
the son of horse-taming Tydeus, strong Diomedes.”
sentences.i: But get up and look, you too; I cannot tell well myself. It seems to me the man is an Aetolian by birth, who is lord among the Argives, the son of Tydeus the horse-tamer, strong Diomedes.”
sentences.n: ἴδεσθε is the aorist imperative middle of ὁράω, ‘look’, and ὔμμες is the Aeolic form of ὑμεῖς. ἀνασταδόν ‘standing up’ is an adverb (they should rise to see). οὐ … εὖ διαγιγνώσκω is ‘I do not tell well’. The man he describes, ἀνὴρ Αἰτωλὸς γενεήν, is ‘an Aetolian by birth’ (accusative of respect), since Tydeus came from Calydon in Aetolia; Idomeneus has in fact guessed right. ἀνάσσει is ‘is lord’, Τυδέος ἱπποδάμου ‘of horse-taming Tydeus’, and κρατερὸς Διομήδης ‘strong Diomedes’ is the stock pair. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αἰσχρῶς ἐνένιπεν Ὀϊλῆος ταχὺς Αἴας·
sentences.l: And him shamefully rebuked swift Ajax, son of Oileus:
sentences.i: Swift Ajax, son of Oileus, rebuked him rudely:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ‘and him’ is Idomeneus. αἰσχρῶς is ‘shamefully, in abusive terms’ and ἐνένιπεν is the imperfect of ἐνίπτω ‘rebuke’. Ὀϊλῆος ταχὺς Αἴας is the stock phrase ‘swift Ajax, son of Oileus’, the lesser Ajax, kept apart from Telamonian Ajax. A new paragraph begins here, with the quarrel over what they see.

sentences.t:
Ἰδομενεῦ τί πάρος λαβρεύεαι; αἳ δέ τ’ ἄνευθεν
ἵπποι ἀερσίποδες πολέος πεδίοιο δίενται.
sentences.l:
“Idomeneus, why do you babble ahead of time? and far off
the foot-lifting horses are speeding over the wide plain.
sentences.i: “Idomeneus, why do you babble before it is time? Far off, the high-stepping horses are speeding across the wide plain.
sentences.n: Ἰδομενεῦ is the vocative. λαβρεύεαι is ‘you babble, you talk wildly’, with the open ending -εαι, and πάρος ‘before’ makes it ‘in advance, too soon’. αἳ δέ τ’ ἄνευθεν is ‘and those, far off’, the horses. ἀερσίποδες is the stock epithet of horses, ‘foot-lifting’, whose exact sense is not certain. δίενται is the present middle of δίεμαι ‘speed, hurry’, and πολέος πεδίοιο is the epic genitive of place, ‘over the wide plain’.

sentences.t:
οὔτε νεώτατός ἐσσι μετ’ Ἀργείοισι τοσοῦτον,
οὔτέ τοι ὀξύτατον κεφαλῆς ἐκδέρκεται ὄσσε·
sentences.l:
You are neither so very much the youngest among the Argives,
nor does the eye look out sharpest from your head;
sentences.i: You are not so very young among the Argives, nor do your eyes see the sharpest from your head;
sentences.n: οὔτε … οὔτε ‘neither … nor’ lists two charges against Idomeneus, who is not the youngest (νεώτατος) by a long way, and whose eyesight is not the keenest. τοσοῦτον is ‘so much’ and goes with the superlative. ὀξύτατον is a neuter adverb ‘most sharply’, κεφαλῆς ‘from your head’ is genitive of place, and ἐκδέρκεται is the present middle of ἐκδέρκομαι ‘look out’, singular because ὄσσε, though dual in form, is a neuter.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αἰεὶ μύθοις λαβρεύεαι· οὐδέ τί σε χρὴ
λαβραγόρην ἔμεναι· πάρα γὰρ καὶ ἀμείνονες ἄλλοι.
sentences.l:
but always with words you babble; and in no way should you
be a babbler; for there are others here better too.
sentences.i: But you are always babbling in words, and it does not become you to be a loose talker, for there are better men here than you.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ αἰεί ‘but always’ turns from his age to his habit. λαβρεύεαι is as in 474, and λαβραγόρην (‘a wild talker’) is the accusative predicate with ἔμεναι (epic infinitive of εἰμί), οὐδέ τί σε χρή being ‘it is in no way necessary for you’, that is, ‘you ought not’. πάρα is πάρεισι, ‘are present’, and ἀμείνονες ἄλλοι is ‘others better’, which is the point of the rebuke.

sentences.t:
ἵπποι δ’ αὐταὶ ἔασι παροίτεραι, αἳ τὸ πάρος περ,
Εὐμήλου, ἐν δ’ αὐτὸς ἔχων εὔληρα βέβηκε.
sentences.l:
The horses themselves are the ones in front, those that were so before,
Eumelus’, and he himself stands in them holding the reins.”
sentences.i: The mares in front are the same ones as before, Eumelus’s, and he himself is up in the chariot holding the reins.”
sentences.n: ἵπποι δ’ αὐταὶ ἔασι παροίτεραι is ‘the very horses are in front’, with ἔασι the epic form of ‘they are’ and αὐταί ‘the very same’. αἳ τὸ πάρος περ is ‘those as before’, referring to the mares in front from the start. Εὐμήλου is ‘Eumelus’s’, in the genitive after the first clause. ἐν δ’ … βέβηκε is ‘has taken his stand in (them)’, the perfect of βαίνω, and εὔληρα, which occurs also in the Odyssey, is a poetic word for ‘reins’. Ajax is mistaken, as the next part will show. The speech ends here, and the part ends at the printed paragraph break.
